label: thm:ftc1
title: First Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be integrable on $[a, b]$ and continuous at a point $x \in [a,b]$, with $x \in (a, b]$ or $x \in [a, b)$ as appropriate. Then the function $F(y) = \int_a^y f(t)\,dt$ has derivative $f(x)$ at $x$. More precisely, in Mathlib this is \texttt{intervalIntegral.integral\_hasDerivAt\_right}, which states that if $f$ is interval integrable on $[a, b]$, and $f$ is continuous at $x$ within $[a, b]$ (via the appropriate one-sided filter), then $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x)$.
proof:
Fix $x$ in the interior of $[a,b]$. We wish to show
\[
  \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{F(x+h) - F(x)}{h} = f(x).
\]
By additivity of the integral,
\[
  F(x+h) - F(x) = \int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,dt,
\]
so
\[
  \frac{F(x+h) - F(x)}{h} - f(x) = \frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h} (f(t) - f(x))\,dt.
\]
By continuity of $f$ at $x$, given $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $|t - x| < \delta$ implies $\|f(t) - f(x)\| < \varepsilon$. For $0 < |h| < \delta$, by the integral bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_bound}),
\[
  \left\|\frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h} (f(t) - f(x))\,dt\right\| \le \varepsilon.
\]
Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, $F'(x) = f(x)$.
